newsitem.title: GERMANY: Vietnamese gang goes on trial for Berlin murders.
newsitem.headline: Vietnamese gang goes on trial for Berlin murders.

text.p: Sixteen Vietnamese went on trial on Friday suspected of belonging to a cigarette-smuggling ring and charged with a string of grisly murders that brought unheard-of gangland violence to Berlin.

But proceedings were broken off after just two hours and before the charge sheet could be read out, because defence lawyers contested the identity of some of the defendants and called for the media to be shut out of court.

Fifteen men and one woman, aged between 18 and 43, stand charged with nine counts of murder and one of kidnapping in a suspected territorial battle for control of a lucrative contraband cigarette racket.
All 16 deny the charges. Among those on trial are the suspected gang leader Le Duy Bao, 26, known in the underworld as Ngoc Thien or "The Merciful", and his 18-year-old girlfriend.

Since Bao was detained last September, along with seven other Vietnamese, Berlin police claim to have broken up the city's notorious "cigarette mafia", which has led to the murder of 40 Vietnamese in the last few years.

Bao's gang, which at its peak had 50 members, stands charged with murdering six asylum-seekers from a rival group, who were tied up and shot in the head in east Berlin last May for refusing to reveal the whereabouts of their boss.
Two others were allegedly killed for concealing profits from Bao and the ninth murder victim was another cigarette-seller who fell foul of his gang.

Police have said Bao's gang was believed to control two-thirds of the 1,200 peddlers selling smuggled cigarettes in Berlin -- a racket thought to cost the government a billion marks ($500 million) a year in lost tax revenues.
The trial began under tight security, the 16 defendants sitting in two special boxes, shielded by bulletproof glass and accompanied by 14 guards.

But proceedings were postponed until next Thursday for the identities of some to be investigated and the court to consider a request for the media to be excluded to protect the identity of Bao's girlfriend, a juvenile at the time of the alleged crimes.

Defence lawyers said the prosecution's case rested largely on the testimony of one Vietnamese woman, who says she witnessed one of the murders. "It is doubtful whether that will be enough for a conviction," said defence lawyer Olaf Franke.

Berlin police last year set up a task force including Vietnamese agents to help them tackle the racketeers, who brought gang warfare to what is normally a relatively safe city and who were smuggling in up to 10 billion cigarettes a year.
The crackdown has succeeded in making the peddlers, whose wares are mostly smuggled in from Poland, a much less common sight on streets in Berlin and other east German cities.

Most of the peddlers were members of a 40,000-strong Vietnamese community -- many of them contract workers sent to East Germany during the Cold War, when Hanoi and Communist East Berlin enjoyed close relations.
Most were left without legal jobs after German unification in 1990 and many got caught up in the vicious turf war between rival Vietnamese gangs dealing in smuggled cigarettes.

Hanoi is gradually honouring an agreement with Bonn to accept forced repatriation of Vietnamese living here illegally. In exchange for taking its citizens back, Bonn gave Vietnam 200 million marks in development aid last year. ($ = 1.865 German Marks)
